28.1.intro: Your first hire should give you back the hours you spend on work that doesn't need you.

steps.say: For two weeks, write down every task and how long it took. Mark each one: only I can do it, someone could do it with a checklist, or it should stop.
steps.check: You have a task log with every task marked.
steps.lost: Write down today's tasks and times.

steps.say: Group the checklist tasks into one role, like customer service, order problems, product uploads and reporting.
steps.check: You have a first role worth about 10 hours a week or more.
steps.lost: Group 3 tasks someone else could do.

steps.say: Write the role as results. Example: "every customer email answered within one business day".
steps.check: Success can be measured.
steps.lost: Write one result for the role.

steps.say: Give shortlisted people a small paid trial task that matches the real work.
steps.check: You see real work before hiring.
steps.lost: Pay for one small test task.

steps.say: Agree terms in writing: hours or deliverables, rate, notice, confidentiality, and that their work belongs to you.
steps.check: A signed agreement exists.
steps.lost: Put the rate and hours in writing.

steps.say: Check if the person is an employee or contractor, based on how the work really happens, not the label.
steps.check: You know which rules apply.
steps.careful: Australia: check the ATO's employee or contractor guide and Fair Work. Super is paid each payday from 1 July 2026. US: the IRS looks at control and independence (W-2 or 1099).
steps.lost: Read the official employee or contractor guide.

28.2.intro: A remote assistant can be a great first hire, if the work is written down and access is safe.

steps.say: Record your screen doing each task once, talking it through. Turn it into a short checklist.
steps.check: Every task has a checklist.
steps.lost: Record one task today.

steps.say: Give the assistant their own logins with only the access they need (Lesson 25.1).
steps.check: No password is shared.
steps.lost: Make them their own login.

steps.say: Agree working hours that overlap with yours for at least an hour a day.
steps.check: You can talk live every day.
steps.lost: Pick one shared hour.

steps.say: Set 3 weekly numbers they own, like reply time, tickets closed and errors.
steps.check: Their results can be measured.
steps.lost: Pick one number: reply time.

steps.say: Meet for 15 minutes each week to look at the numbers and update checklists.
steps.check: Checklists get better each week.
steps.lost: Book a 15-minute weekly chat.

steps.say: Pay on time, in their currency if you can, with a method you can track.
steps.check: Payments are on time and recorded.
steps.careful: Check market rates for the skill and country, and pay fairly. Underpaid assistants leave fast.
steps.lost: Set a regular pay day.

steps.say: When they leave, remove their access the same day.
steps.check: Former staff have no access.
steps.lost: Remove access on their last day.

28.3.intro: Creators get paid with free product, a flat fee, commission, or a mix. Clear written terms stop arguments later. Lesson 19.4 covers rates.

steps.say: Split every quote into parts: making the content, posting it, usage rights (using it in your ads, and for how long), exclusivity, and raw footage.
steps.check: You know what each part costs.
steps.lost: Ask: what's the price for usage rights?

steps.say: Put it in writing: deliverables, dates, revisions, usage rights, payment date, and what happens if a post is late.
steps.check: Every deal has a written agreement.
steps.lost: Write the dates and the payment.

steps.say: Count gifting costs (product, shipping, your time) when you compare it with paid work.
steps.check: You compare deals fairly.
steps.lost: Add up product + shipping for one gift.

steps.say: Make sure every paid or gifted post is clearly labelled as an ad.
steps.check: All posts are disclosed.
steps.careful: Australia: follow the ACCC's influencer guidance. GST registered creators add GST. US: follow the FTC's disclosure guide. Creators paid $2,000 or more in 2026 usually need a 1099-NEC (Lesson 27.6).
steps.lost: Ask them to add "ad" to the post.

steps.say: Pay on time and keep invoices.
steps.check: Records are complete.
steps.lost: Save the invoice.

steps.say: Track each creator's sales from their code or link, and how their content does as an ad.
steps.check: You know which creators to book again.
steps.lost: Check sales from one creator's code.

28.4.intro: When you pay in another currency, the exchange rate margin can cost more than the bank fee. Scams also target importers, so check before you pay.

steps.say: For one real payment, compare the total cost with your bank and at least one money transfer provider: your rate against the mid-market rate, plus fees.
steps.check: You know the cheapest way to pay.
steps.lost: Compare one payment two ways.

steps.say: Pay in the supplier's currency when that's cheaper than letting them convert.
steps.check: You avoid converting twice.
steps.lost: Ask which currency is cheaper.

steps.say: Agree payment terms in writing: deposit, balance timing, and what happens if goods are late or faulty (Lesson 14.8).
steps.check: Terms are written down.
steps.lost: Write the deposit and balance dates.

steps.say: Before any first payment, or change of bank details, call the supplier on a number you already have to confirm the account.
steps.check: Bank details are checked by phone.
steps.careful: Never trust new bank details sent only by email. Report scams to Scamwatch (Australia) or the FTC (US).
steps.lost: New bank details? Call them first.

steps.say: If paying by card, check surcharges and your card's foreign transaction fee.
steps.check: You know the card's true cost.
steps.lost: Check your card's foreign fee.

steps.say: For big payments due months ahead, ask your provider about fixing a rate in advance.
steps.check: Your future cost is locked in.
steps.lost: Ask about fixing the rate.

28.5.intro: Loans and cash advances can fund stock for a product that already sells. They make things worse when they fund losses. See Lesson 14.5 too.

steps.say: Write down exactly what you'd buy and how it pays back. Example: more stock of a product that already sells at a profit.
steps.check: You have a clear use for the money.
steps.lost: Write one line: what the money is for.

steps.say: For each offer, write the amount you get, the total you repay, the share of daily sales taken, and the expected repayment time.
steps.check: Offers sit side by side.
steps.lost: Write amount in and total out.

steps.say: Work out the true cost: (total repaid − amount received) ÷ amount received. Example: ($11,000 − $10,000) ÷ $10,000 = 10%. Then think about speed.
steps.check: You know the real cost. A flat fee repaid in 4 months costs far more per year than over 12 months.
steps.lost: Extra you pay ÷ what you get.

steps.say: Check what happens if sales drop. Share-of-sales repayments slow down. Fixed weekly ones don't.
steps.check: You know your downside.
steps.lost: Ask: what if sales drop?

steps.say: Add repayments to your cash forecast before you sign.
steps.check: You can afford it even if sales drop by a quarter.
steps.lost: Add repayments to your cash sheet.

steps.say: Read for personal guarantees, early repayment rules, and what the lender can take if you stop paying.
steps.check: There are no hidden traps.
steps.careful: Look at business.gov.au grants (Australia) and SBA loans (US).
steps.lost: Look for "personal guarantee" in the contract.

28.6.intro: App and tool bills creep up quietly. Many charge by contacts, orders or users, so the bill grows with you.

steps.say: Each quarter, export card and bank statements. List every subscription with its monthly cost.
steps.check: You have a full list of tools and costs.
steps.lost: List 5 subscriptions you pay for.

steps.say: For each tool, write what it does for sales or time saved. Cancel anything you can't justify.
steps.check: Only useful tools are left.
steps.careful: Uninstall apps properly in Shopify. Some leave code or keep billing.
steps.lost: Cancel one tool you don't need.

steps.say: Remove email and SMS contacts who haven't opened or clicked for a long time, after one last win-back message (Module 10).
steps.check: Your contact-based bill drops.
steps.lost: Send a win-back email, then remove the quiet ones.

steps.say: Check plan limits before a big sale.
steps.check: No surprise jump to a pricier plan.
steps.lost: Check your email plan limit.

steps.say: Pay yearly only for tools you're sure to keep.
steps.check: You're not locked into tools you drop.
steps.lost: Not sure? Pay monthly.

steps.say: Enter total tool costs in your Helix monthly fixed costs.
steps.check: Net profit includes tools.
steps.lost: Add tool costs to fixed costs.

28.7.intro: Running a store can be lonely, and money worries can keep you up. Looking after yourself is part of the job.

steps.say: Look at numbers on a schedule: profit each morning in Helix, cash once a week.
steps.check: Small regular check-ins replace dread.
steps.lost: Check profit once this morning.

steps.say: Keep a cash buffer you don't touch, even a small one.
steps.check: You know there's a safety net.
steps.lost: Put a little aside today.

steps.say: Write down your 3 biggest worries, and one small next step for each.
steps.check: Each worry has an action.
steps.lost: Write one worry and one small step.

steps.say: Protect sleep, movement, and at least one day a week away from the business.
steps.check: One day off a week is in your calendar.
steps.lost: Pick your day off.

steps.say: Talk to someone: a friend, a peer, a mentor or a professional. Don't wait for a crisis.
steps.check: You have someone to call this week.
steps.lost: Message one person today.

steps.say: Hand off one draining task this month (Lesson 28.1).
steps.check: One task is off your plate.
steps.lost: Pick one task to hand off.

28.8.intro: Amazon can add sales, but it has its own fees, rules and competition. Decide with numbers.

steps.say: Search Amazon for your product type. Note prices, review counts, and whether copies already exist.
steps.check: You know the competition.
steps.careful: Australia's Amazon marketplace is smaller than the US one, so check demand first.
steps.lost: Search Amazon for your product.

steps.say: Use Amazon's fee calculator to work out profit per unit: price minus referral fee, fulfilment fee, storage, ads and returns.
steps.check: You know profit per unit after all fees.
steps.lost: Put your best seller in the fee calculator.

steps.say: Choose how to sell: as a seller (you set prices and listings) or, if invited, as a wholesale supplier to Amazon.
steps.check: You have a selling model.
steps.lost: Most start as a seller.

steps.say: Register your trademark and enrol in Amazon's brand registry before you list.
steps.check: Your brand is protected.
steps.lost: Register your trademark first.

steps.say: List only your best seller first. Keep its stock separate.
steps.check: Your own store never runs out.
steps.lost: List one product.

steps.say: After 90 days, look at profit, the effect on your own store, and time spent.
steps.check: You have a keep or stop decision. Marketplaces usually collect US sales tax for you (Lesson 26.3).
steps.lost: Put a 90-day review in your calendar.

28.9.intro: Shops that stock your product reach people who never see your ads. Less profit per unit, but bigger orders and no ad cost per sale.

steps.say: Work out your wholesale price. Most shops expect to buy at about half the retail price. Example: $40 retail, about $20 wholesale. Check in your profit setup that landed cost, packaging and freight still leave a profit.
steps.check: A wholesale price for each product that still makes money, or a list of products that can't be sold wholesale.
steps.lost: Retail ÷ 2. Does it still make a profit?

steps.say: Write simple terms on one page: minimum order, payment terms (upfront for first orders), delivery times, and a promise not to undercut your stockists on your own site outside planned sales.
steps.check: A one-page wholesale terms sheet.
steps.lost: Write the minimum order and payment terms.

steps.say: List 20 independent shops whose customers match yours. Send each a short, personal email with photos, prices and your terms. Offer a small first order.
steps.check: 20 shops contacted, with replies tracked in a simple sheet.
steps.lost: Email 5 shops this week.

steps.say: Set up wholesale ordering in Shopify (a separate price list or a wholesale app). Keep wholesale stock separate in your stock check.
steps.check: Stockists can reorder without lots of emails, and retail stock is protected.
steps.careful: Big chains can ask for long payment terms, returns of unsold stock and heavy discounts. Start with independent shops, and only say yes to terms your cash flow can carry.
steps.lost: Make one wholesale price list.
